record.paper_title: Some open problems on the analysis of the Cauchy-Fueter system in several variables
record.context_brief: Taylor expansions in several quaternionic variables
record.original_question: For regular functions of several quaternionic variables, can one prove an analogue of the one-variable Taylor expansion theorem? Here H denotes the quaternion algebra; a regular function of n quaternionic variables is a differentiable function f: H^n -> H satisfying the left Cauchy-Fueter equation d f / d bar(q_i) = 0 in every variable. The one-variable theory uses homogeneous regular polynomials P_nu and the Cauchy-Kowalewski (C-K) product, which multiplies entire regular functions while staying regular; no analogous C-K product is known in several variables, and this absence blocks a Taylor series theory.

evidence.quote: An analogous C-K product is not known in the case of several variables; this fact prevents us from defining a Taylor series for regular functions defined on H^n.
We would like to point out that it is not known if it is possible to prove an analogous theorem to the case of regular functions of several quaternionic variables.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{H}$ denote the algebra of real quaternions with standard basis $1, i, j, k$, and write a quaternion as $q = x_0 + x_1 i + x_2 j + x_3 k$. For a differentiable function $f : \mathbb{H} \to \mathbb{H}$, define the left Cauchy–Fueter operator by
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial \bar{q}} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_0} + i\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} + j\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} + k\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_3}.$$
A differentiable function $f : \mathbb{H}^n \to \mathbb{H}$ in variables $q_1, \dots, q_n \in \mathbb{H}$ is called (left) regular if it satisfies the Cauchy–Fueter equation in each variable separately, i.e.
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial \bar{q}_i} = 0, \qquad i = 1, \dots, n.$$
In the one-variable case ($n = 1$), Fueter's theorem states that every regular function $f$ defined on a suitable neighborhood of the origin admits a Taylor-type expansion
$$f(q) = \sum_{\nu} P_\nu(q)\, a_\nu,$$
where $\{P_\nu\}$ is the family of homogeneous regular polynomials in $q$ and $a_\nu \in \mathbb{H}$. A key ingredient enabling the construction and multiplication of regular functions in this one-variable theory is the Cauchy–Kowalewski (C–K) product, which assigns to two entire regular functions a new entire regular function and which restricts to the usual product on the subspace $\{q : x_0 = 0\}$.

Problem. Establish, or refute, an analogue of the Taylor expansion theorem for regular functions of several quaternionic variables: namely, prove that every regular function $f : \Omega \subseteq \mathbb{H}^n \to \mathbb{H}$, with $\Omega$ a suitable neighborhood of the origin, can be expanded as a convergent series
$$f(q_1, \dots, q_n) = \sum_{\nu} P_\nu(q_1, \dots, q_n)\, a_\nu, \qquad a_\nu \in \mathbb{H},$$
in terms of a natural family of homogeneous regular polynomials $P_\nu$ on $\mathbb{H}^n$. Equivalently, construct a multivariable analogue of the Cauchy–Kowalewski product on entire regular functions of $n$ quaternionic variables that allows such a Taylor theory to be developed.

status_evidence.title: Cauchy-Fueter system in several variables
status_evidence.snippet: Discussion of regularity in several quaternionic variables; no multivariable C-K product analogue described.
status_evidence.claim: The multivariable Cauchy-Fueter setting lacks a Cauchy-Kowalewski product, leaving Taylor expansion in several variables unsettled.

status_evidence.title: The Cauchy-Fueter System and Its Variations
status_evidence.snippet: Survey of Cauchy-Fueter system; one-variable Taylor theory relies on C-K product.
status_evidence.claim: No analogue of the C-K product in several variables is known, blocking a Taylor series theory.

artifact.status_search_result: A web search did not turn up a known proof of a multivariable Taylor expansion theorem for regular functions on $\mathbb{H}^n$, nor a construction of a multivariable Cauchy–Kowalewski product. Available surveys on the Cauchy–Fueter system in several variables continue to treat the absence of such a product as an obstruction, so the problem appears to remain open.
